summary: Keyflower blends tile auctions with worker placement across four seasonal rounds, where colored workers both bid for new village tiles and activate abilities on any tile at the table — including opponents'. It rewards reading the auction carefully and squeezing value from other players' villages as much as building up your own.
praised: brilliant mechanism of activating others' tiles
strong tension in the winter round when workers can't leave
high replayability from modular tile setup
scales well to higher player counts
criticised: fiddly bookkeeping with many worker colors and tile abilities
upkeep tracking who benefits from which tile action

interaction.kind: bidding against opponents for shared tiles, and sending your own workers onto opponents' villages to use their tile abilities
interaction.detail: Any tile up for auction can be won by an opponent, and crucially, workers of a matching color can be used on tiles in any player's village, not just your own, so opponents constantly benefit from or disrupt each other's boards. Combined with the endgame's frantic bidding and the ability to outbid someone right as they're about to activate a key tile, most of the game plays out through direct contests over the same shared tiles.
interaction.said: commonly called cutthroat and mean, especially in the winter round; players talk about "working other people's tiles" and bidding wars that can strip a rival's key tile away

subsystems: village tile collection and worker-driven tile abilities
sources: VP from skill-tile scoring conditions triggered at game end
VP from leftover resources/gold converted at game end
VP from remaining workers of certain colors
scoring.how_you_win: Over four seasonal rounds, players bid colored workers to win tiles for their village or use workers to activate tile abilities (their own or others') that generate resources and skills; at the end of winter, tile VP, skill bonuses, and converted leftover resources are totaled and the highest score wins.
